cards.english: How do you write a for loop?
How do you transform every item in an array? (JavaScript)
cards.code: const doubled = nums.map((n) => n * 2);

cards.english: How do you build a list from a range with a transform? (Python)
cards.code: squares = [x * x for x in range(10)]

cards.english: Why use a hash map / hash set?
cards.word: O(1) average insert, delete, and lookup
cards.grammarNote: Hash structures trade memory for speed: they turn 'have I seen this?' or 'what maps to this key?' into **O(1) average** operations, replacing O(n) scans. The cost is O(n) extra space and O(n) worst case under heavy collisions.

cards.english: What are the time complexities of basic array operations?
cards.word: Access O(1), search O(n), insert/delete O(n) (end is amortized O(1))
cards.grammarNote: Random access by index is **O(1)**. Searching an unsorted array is **O(n)**. Inserting/removing in the middle shifts elements → **O(n)**; appending to a dynamic array is amortized **O(1)**.

cards.english: Contains Duplicate — return true if any value appears more than once.
cards.grammarNote: Track seen values in a **Set**; a repeat means a duplicate. **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space.

cards.english: Valid Anagram — is t a rearrangement of the characters of s?
cards.grammarNote: Anagrams have identical character counts. Tally s, then decrement for t. **O(n)** time; **O(1)** space if limited to a fixed alphabet (else O(n)).

cards.english: Two Sum — return indices of the two numbers that add up to target.
cards.grammarNote: One pass: for each number, check if its **complement** (target - n) was already seen. **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space — beats the O(n²) brute force.

cards.english: Group Anagrams — group words that are anagrams of each other.
cards.grammarNote: Key each word by its **char-count signature** so anagrams share a key. **O(m·n)** for m words of avg length n. (Sorting each word as the key is O(m·n log n).)

cards.english: Top K Frequent Elements — return the k most frequent values.
cards.grammarNote: **Bucket sort by frequency**: index i holds all values seen i times. Scan buckets high→low. **O(n)** time — better than the O(n log n) heap approach.

cards.english: Encode and Decode Strings — serialize a list of strings and parse it back.
cards.grammarNote: **Length-prefix** each string as `len#content`. The length tells the decoder exactly how many chars to read, so `#` inside content is safe. **O(n)** both ways.

cards.english: Product of Array Except Self — output[i] = product of all elements except nums[i] (no division).
cards.grammarNote: Each answer is (product of everything left) × (product of everything right). Two passes accumulate **prefix** then **postfix** products. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** extra space (output excluded).

cards.english: Longest Consecutive Sequence — length of the longest run of consecutive integers (unsorted).
cards.grammarNote: Put everything in a Set. Only begin counting when `n-1` is absent (a sequence **start**), so each element is visited once overall. **O(n)** time — no sorting needed.

cards.english: When does the two-pointer pattern apply?
cards.word: Sorted arrays, palindromes, or pair/triplet searches
cards.grammarNote: Two pointers converge from both ends (or move at different speeds) to replace a nested loop, dropping **O(n²)** to **O(n)**. It usually needs a **sorted** input or a symmetric structure so you know which pointer to move.

cards.english: What's the space complexity of most two-pointer solutions?
cards.word: O(1) — just a couple of index variables
cards.grammarNote: The pattern mutates indices in place rather than allocating extra structures, so extra space is **O(1)** (excluding the output).

cards.english: Valid Palindrome — ignoring non-alphanumerics and case, is the string a palindrome?
cards.grammarNote: Converge two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric chars and comparing case-insensitively. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: 3Sum — all unique triplets that sum to zero.
cards.grammarNote: **Sort**, then fix each anchor and two-pointer the rest (like 2Sum). Skip duplicates for both the anchor and the moved pointer. **O(n²)** time, O(1)/O(n) space.

cards.english: Container With Most Water — max area between two vertical lines.
cards.grammarNote: Start wide; area is width × the **shorter** wall. Moving the taller wall can never help, so always move the shorter pointer inward. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: What is the sliding-window technique and when do you use it?
cards.word: A moving sub-range over contiguous data — O(n) instead of O(n²)
cards.grammarNote: Maintain a window [l, r] and update an aggregate as it grows/shrinks, so each element is added and removed at most once → **O(n)**. Use it for **contiguous** subarray/substring problems (longest/shortest/max-sum satisfying a constraint).

cards.english: What's the difference between a fixed and a dynamic sliding window?
cards.word: Fixed = constant size k; dynamic = grows/shrinks to stay valid
cards.grammarNote: A **fixed** window slides one step at a time (e.g. max sum of k elements). A **dynamic** window expands the right edge and contracts the left whenever a constraint is violated (e.g. longest substring without repeats).

cards.english: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock — max profit from one buy then one later sell.
cards.grammarNote: Track the **lowest price so far** (buy day); at each day the best profit is price − min. One pass, **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters.
cards.grammarNote: Expand the right edge; when a repeat appears, shrink from the left until the window is valid again. Each char enters/leaves once → **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Longest Repeating Character Replacement — longest same-char substring after ≤ k replacements.
cards.grammarNote: A window is valid when (window length − count of its **most frequent** char) ≤ k (the rest can be replaced). Shrink when invalid. **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Minimum Window Substring — smallest substring of s containing all chars of t.
cards.grammarNote: Track `have`/`need` = how many required chars are currently satisfied. Grow right until valid, then shrink left to minimize while still valid. **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Why and when would you use a stack?
cards.word: LIFO — matching, monotonic scans, DFS, undo/backtracking
cards.grammarNote: A stack (**last-in, first-out**) shines when the most recent item is what you need next: bracket matching, next-greater-element (monotonic stack), expression parsing, iterative DFS, and undo history.

cards.english: What are the complexities of stack operations?
cards.word: push / pop / peek are O(1); space O(n)
cards.grammarNote: Backed by an array or linked list, all core operations are **O(1)**. Space is **O(n)** for the elements held.

cards.english: Valid Parentheses — are ()[]{} correctly matched and nested?
cards.grammarNote: Push opens onto a **stack**; on a closer, the top must be its matching opener (else invalid). Valid iff the stack ends empty. **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space.

cards.english: When can you use binary search?
cards.word: On a sorted array or any monotonic search space — O(log n)
cards.grammarNote: Binary search halves the search space each step, giving **O(log n)**. It needs a **monotonic** predicate: sorted data, or a 'smallest x that satisfies P' answer space where P flips false→true exactly once.

cards.english: What are common binary-search pitfalls?
cards.word: Wrong loop bound, mid overflow, and infinite loops
cards.grammarNote: Watch the invariant: `l <= r` vs `l < r`, whether to use `m-1`/`m+1` or keep `m`, and computing mid as `l + ((r-l)>>1)` to avoid overflow. Getting the shrink step wrong causes infinite loops.

cards.english: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (distinct values).
cards.grammarNote: The minimum is the rotation point. Binary search toward the **unsorted** half. If the current slice is already sorted, its left end is the answer. **O(log n)** time.

cards.english: Search in Rotated Sorted Array — return index of target, or -1.
cards.grammarNote: Each step, one half is sorted. Decide whether target lies inside that sorted half; if so search it, otherwise search the other half. **O(log n)** time.

cards.english: Why use a linked list instead of an array?
cards.word: O(1) insert/delete at a known node; no shifting; grows dynamically
cards.grammarNote: Linked lists give **O(1)** insertion/removal once you hold the node (no element shifting) and grow without reallocation. The trade-off: **no random access** (indexing is O(n)) and worse cache locality than arrays.

cards.english: What are the time complexities of linked-list operations?
cards.word: Access/search O(n); insert/delete at head O(1)
cards.grammarNote: Reaching the i-th node requires walking from the head → **O(n)** access and search. Inserting/deleting at the **head** (or at a node you already reference) is **O(1)**.

cards.english: What is a dummy (sentinel) node and why use it?
cards.word: A placeholder before the head that removes edge cases
cards.grammarNote: A dummy node lets you treat the real head like any other node, so operations that might change the head (insert/remove at front, merges) need no special-casing. Return `dummy.next` at the end.

cards.english: Reverse Linked List — reverse a singly linked list.
cards.grammarNote: Walk the list, flipping each `next` pointer to the previous node. `prev` ends on the new head. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Merge Two Sorted Lists — merge into one sorted list.
cards.grammarNote: A **dummy head** avoids edge cases. Repeatedly append the smaller node, then attach whatever list remains. **O(n + m)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Linked List Cycle — does the list contain a cycle?
cards.grammarNote: **Floyd's tortoise & hare**: a fast pointer (2 steps) laps a slow one (1 step) inside any cycle, so they meet. No extra memory. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Reorder List — L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→L2… in place.
cards.grammarNote: Three steps: find the middle (slow/fast), **reverse** the second half, then **interleave** the two halves. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Remove Nth Node From End of List.
cards.grammarNote: Two pointers a fixed **gap of n** apart: when `right` reaches the end, `left` sits just before the target. A dummy head handles removing the first node. **O(n)** time, one pass.

cards.english: Merge K Sorted Lists — merge k sorted lists into one.
cards.grammarNote: **Pairwise merge**: merge lists two at a time, halving the count each round (like merge sort). **O(n log k)** time for n total nodes across k lists — better than merging them one-by-one (O(n·k)).

cards.english: What are the tree traversals and their complexity?
cards.word: DFS (pre/in/post) and BFS (level-order) — all O(n) time
cards.grammarNote: **DFS** visits deep first (preorder root-left-right, inorder left-root-right, postorder left-right-root); **BFS** visits level by level with a queue. All are **O(n)** time. Space is **O(h)** for DFS (recursion/stack) and **O(w)** for BFS (widest level).

cards.english: What defines a binary search tree, and what are its complexities?
cards.word: left < node < right; search/insert/delete O(h) — O(log n) balanced
cards.grammarNote: In a BST every left descendant is smaller and every right larger, so an **inorder** traversal is sorted. Operations are **O(h)**: **O(log n)** when balanced, but **O(n)** if the tree degenerates into a chain (hence self-balancing trees).

cards.english: Why are so many tree problems solved with recursion?
cards.word: A tree is defined recursively, so subtrees are the same subproblem
cards.grammarNote: Each node's answer is a function of its children's answers, matching the recursive structure directly. The call stack naturally implements DFS; just define the base case (null) and combine child results.

cards.english: Invert Binary Tree — mirror it left↔right.
cards.grammarNote: Swap the two children at every node (recursively). **O(n)** time, **O(h)** stack space.

cards.english: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree.
cards.grammarNote: Depth = 1 + the deeper child's depth. Classic postorder recursion. **O(n)** time, **O(h)** space.

cards.english: Same Tree — are two trees structurally identical with equal values?
cards.grammarNote: Compare nodes in lockstep: both null = equal, one null or values differ = not, else recurse both sides. **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Subtree of Another Tree — is subRoot a subtree of root?
cards.grammarNote: At each node, test `isSameTree`; otherwise recurse into children. **O(m·n)** worst case (m = root size, n = subRoot size).

cards.english: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST.
cards.grammarNote: Use the BST order: if both targets are larger go right, if both smaller go left; the first node where they diverge (or equals one) is the LCA. **O(h)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (BFS).
cards.grammarNote: BFS one level at a time: process the whole current queue, collecting the next level as you go. **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space.

cards.english: Validate Binary Search Tree.
cards.grammarNote: Pass down an allowed (min, max) range and tighten it as you descend — a node must fall strictly inside. Checking only parent-child isn't enough. **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Kth Smallest Element in a BST.
cards.grammarNote: An **inorder** traversal of a BST yields sorted values; stop at the k-th. Iterative with an explicit stack. **O(h + k)** time.

cards.english: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal.
cards.grammarNote: Preorder gives the root order; the root's index in inorder splits left/right subtrees. A value→index map makes the split O(1). **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (path may not pass through root).
cards.grammarNote: At each node, the best **split** path is node + max(0,left) + max(0,right); update the global max. Return only the best single branch upward (a parent can't use both). **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.
cards.grammarNote: Preorder DFS with explicit **null markers** ('N') captures structure unambiguously; deserialization consumes tokens in the same order. **O(n)** both ways.

cards.english: What is a heap and what are its complexities?
cards.word: A complete binary tree: push/pop O(log n), peek O(1), build O(n)
cards.grammarNote: A binary heap keeps the min (or max) at the root via the heap property. **push** and **pop** are **O(log n)** (sift up/down), **peek** is **O(1)**, and building from n items is **O(n)**. It's the backing structure of a priority queue.

cards.english: When should you reach for a heap?
cards.word: Top-k, streaming medians, scheduling, and Dijkstra
cards.grammarNote: Use a heap whenever you repeatedly need the current min/max from a changing set: **top-k frequent**, **k-th largest**, merging k lists, event scheduling, and shortest-path (Dijkstra). Note: **JavaScript has no built-in heap**, so you implement one or use two heaps.

cards.english: Find Median from Data Stream (JS has no built-in heap).
cards.grammarNote: Keep two heaps: a **max-heap** for the lower half and a **min-heap** for the upper half, balanced to differ in size by ≤ 1. The median is a heap top (or the average of both). **addNum O(log n)**, **findMedian O(1)**.

cards.english: What is backtracking?
cards.word: DFS over choices that undoes each choice as it unwinds
cards.grammarNote: Backtracking builds a candidate incrementally, recursing on each **choice**, then **undoing** it (pop) before trying the next. Pruning invalid branches early is what makes it tractable. It's the go-to for subsets, permutations, combinations, and grid path search.

cards.english: What's the typical time complexity of backtracking?
cards.word: Exponential — often O(2^n), O(n!), or O(k^n)
cards.grammarNote: You explore a decision tree, so cost scales with the number of candidates: **O(2^n)** for subsets, **O(n!)** for permutations. Pruning cuts the constant/branches but the worst case stays exponential.

cards.english: Combination Sum — all combinations summing to target (numbers reusable).
cards.grammarNote: At each index, branch: **use** the current number (stay at i so it can repeat) or **skip** it (i+1). Push/pop to backtrack; prune when the total exceeds target. Exponential time.

cards.english: Word Search — does the word exist along adjacent cells?
cards.grammarNote: DFS from each cell, matching characters and marking cells visited in place to prevent reuse, then restoring on backtrack. **O(m·n·4^L)** time for word length L.

cards.english: What is a trie and why use it?
cards.word: A prefix tree: insert/search a word in O(L) by its length
cards.grammarNote: A trie stores strings by shared **prefixes**, one node per character. Insert and search are **O(L)** (word length), independent of how many words are stored — ideal for autocomplete, prefix queries, and dictionary lookups.

cards.english: What's the trade-off of a trie?
cards.word: Fast prefix ops at the cost of high memory
cards.grammarNote: Each node holds up to an alphabet's worth of child pointers, so a trie can use far more memory than a hash set — you're paying space to make **prefix** operations fast and to avoid rehashing whole strings.

cards.english: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) — insert / search / startsWith.
cards.grammarNote: Each node holds a map of children and an `end` flag. Walk/create nodes per character. `search` needs the end flag; `startsWith` just needs the path to exist. All ops **O(L)**.

cards.english: Design Add and Search Words — search supports '.' wildcard.
cards.grammarNote: A trie plus DFS: on a normal char follow the single edge; on '.' branch into **all** children and recurse. Worst case (all dots) is O(26^L), otherwise O(L).

cards.english: Word Search II — find all dictionary words in the grid.
cards.grammarNote: Build a trie of all words, then DFS the grid **once**, advancing the trie pointer instead of testing each word separately. Null out a node's word after collecting it to dedupe. Far faster than searching each word individually.

cards.english: How do you represent a graph, and what's the trade-off?
cards.word: Adjacency list O(V+E) space vs adjacency matrix O(V²)
cards.grammarNote: An **adjacency list** (map/array of neighbor lists) is compact for sparse graphs and iterates neighbors efficiently. An **adjacency matrix** gives O(1) edge checks but O(V²) space — better for dense graphs.

cards.english: BFS vs DFS on a graph — when do you use each?
cards.word: BFS = shortest path (unweighted); DFS = connectivity, cycles, topo sort
cards.grammarNote: **BFS** (queue) finds the fewest-edges path and explores by distance. **DFS** (stack/recursion) is natural for connected components, cycle detection, and topological sort. Both are **O(V+E)**.

cards.english: How do you avoid infinite loops when traversing a graph?
cards.word: Track visited nodes in a set/array
cards.grammarNote: Unlike trees, graphs have cycles, so you must mark nodes **visited** before/when enqueuing or recursing. Forgetting this causes infinite loops and redundant work.

cards.english: Number of Islands — count connected groups of '1'.
cards.grammarNote: Each unvisited '1' starts a new island; flood-fill (DFS/BFS) sinks its whole component so it's counted once. **O(m·n)** time.

cards.english: Clone Graph — deep copy an undirected graph.
cards.grammarNote: DFS while memoizing original→copy so each node is cloned once and cycles terminate. Wire up neighbors from the map. **O(V+E)** time.

cards.english: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow — cells that can reach both oceans.
cards.grammarNote: Reverse the flow: DFS **inward** from each ocean's border, moving only to cells of equal-or-greater height. Cells reachable from **both** oceans are the answer. **O(m·n)** time.

cards.english: Course Schedule — can all courses be finished (cycle detection)?
cards.grammarNote: The graph is finishable iff it's a **DAG** (no cycle). DFS with three states detects a back edge into a node still being visited. **O(V+E)** time.

cards.english: Graph Valid Tree — is the graph a valid tree?
cards.grammarNote: A tree is **connected** and **acyclic**. With exactly n-1 edges, connectivity implies no cycle — so check n-1 edges, then that one DFS reaches all n nodes. **O(V+E)** time.

cards.english: Number of Connected Components (union-find).
cards.grammarNote: **Union-Find**: start with n components; each edge that joins two *different* sets reduces the count. Path compression + union by rank give near-**O(1)** amortized per op.

cards.english: What is topological sort and when do you use it?
cards.word: A linear ordering of a DAG respecting all edges — O(V+E)
cards.grammarNote: Topological sort orders nodes so every edge u→v has u before v. It only exists for a **DAG** (no cycles). Compute it with DFS post-order (reversed) or Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly remove indegree-0 nodes). Used for build/task/course ordering.

cards.english: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
cards.word: DFS with three states: unvisited / in-progress / done
cards.grammarNote: During DFS, mark a node **in-progress**; if you reach a node that's still in-progress, there's a **back edge** = cycle. Mark **done** when its subtree finishes. (In Kahn's algorithm, a cycle exists if you can't process all nodes.)

cards.english: Alien Dictionary — derive char order from sorted words (topological sort).
cards.grammarNote: Each adjacent word pair gives one ordering edge (first differing char). Then **topological sort** via DFS post-order; a cycle means no valid order. Watch the invalid-prefix edge case. **O(total chars)** time.

cards.english: What is dynamic programming?
cards.word: Solve overlapping subproblems once via memoization or tabulation
cards.grammarNote: DP applies when a problem has **overlapping subproblems** and **optimal substructure**. Cache each subproblem's result — **top-down** (recursion + memo) or **bottom-up** (fill a table) — to avoid recomputation, turning exponential recursion into polynomial time.

cards.english: How do you recognize a DP problem?
cards.word: Counting ways, or optimizing (min/max) with a choice at each step
cards.grammarNote: Signals: 'how many ways', 'min/max cost', or 'can you reach', where each step has choices and the answer builds on smaller instances. If a greedy choice can fail and you'd otherwise brute-force all combinations, it's likely DP.

cards.english: How can you optimize DP space?
cards.word: Keep only the last few states instead of the whole table
cards.grammarNote: When dp[i] depends only on dp[i-1] (and maybe dp[i-2]), you can drop the array and track a couple of rolling variables, reducing space from **O(n)** to **O(1)** (e.g. Fibonacci, House Robber).

cards.english: Climbing Stairs — ways to reach step n taking 1 or 2 steps.
cards.grammarNote: Ways(n) = Ways(n-1) + Ways(n-2) — it's Fibonacci. Roll two variables instead of an array. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: House Robber — max sum with no two adjacent houses.
cards.grammarNote: At each house choose max(skip = curr, rob = prev + n). Two rolling variables hold the best up to i-1 and i. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: House Robber II — houses are in a circle.
cards.grammarNote: The first and last houses are now adjacent, so run the linear House Robber twice — once excluding the first house, once excluding the last — and take the max. **O(n)** time.

cards.english: Longest Palindromic Substring.
cards.grammarNote: **Expand around center**: every palindrome has a center (a char or a gap). Grow outward from each of the 2n-1 centers. **O(n²)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Palindromic Substrings — count all palindromic substrings.
cards.grammarNote: Same expand-around-center idea, but count each successful expansion instead of tracking the longest. **O(n²)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Decode Ways — number of ways to decode a digit string (A=1…Z=26).
cards.grammarNote: From index i you can consume one digit (if not '0') or two (if 10–26). Sum both branches; memoize by index. **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space.

cards.english: Coin Change — fewest coins to make amount.
cards.grammarNote: Bottom-up: dp[a] = min coins for amount a = 1 + min over coins of dp[a-coin]. Unbounded knapsack style. **O(amount · coins)** time.

cards.english: Maximum Product Subarray.
cards.grammarNote: Track both the running **max and min** products, since a negative number flips them. Reset via `Math.max/min(n, …)` when the streak breaks. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Word Break — can s be segmented into dictionary words?
cards.grammarNote: dp[i] = can the suffix starting at i be segmented. It's true if some prefix s[i..j) is a word and dp[j] is true. Work right to left. **O(n²·L)** time.

cards.english: Longest Increasing Subsequence.
cards.grammarNote: dp[i] = length of the LIS starting at i = 1 + max dp[j] for later, larger elements. **O(n²)** time. (A patience-sorting + binary-search approach does it in **O(n log n)**.)

cards.english: When do you need a 2-D DP table?
cards.word: State depends on two indices — two sequences or a grid
cards.grammarNote: Use a 2-D table when a subproblem is identified by **two** dimensions: positions in two strings (edit distance, LCS) or a cell in a grid (unique paths). dp[i][j] combines neighboring states.

cards.english: What's the typical complexity of grid/2-sequence DP?
cards.word: O(m·n) time and space (often reducible to O(n) space)
cards.grammarNote: You fill an m×n table once → **O(m·n)** time and space. If each row depends only on the previous row, you can keep just one or two rows and cut space to **O(n)**.

cards.english: Unique Paths — count paths from top-left to bottom-right (right/down only).
cards.grammarNote: Paths to a cell = paths from above + paths from the left. Only the previous row is needed, so a single rolling row gives **O(m·n)** time, **O(n)** space.

cards.english: Longest Common Subsequence.
cards.grammarNote: dp[i][j] = LCS of the suffixes from i and j. On a match, add 1 and move both; otherwise take the better of skipping one char from either string. **O(m·n)** time and space.

cards.english: What is a greedy algorithm and when does it work?
cards.word: Take the locally optimal choice; works given the greedy-choice property
cards.grammarNote: A greedy algorithm commits to the best-looking option at each step without reconsidering. It's correct only when the problem has the **greedy-choice property** and **optimal substructure** (e.g. interval scheduling, Kadane's). Otherwise it can miss the global optimum.

cards.english: How does greedy differ from dynamic programming?
cards.word: Greedy commits per step; DP explores all sub-solutions
cards.grammarNote: Greedy makes one irrevocable choice per step (**O(n log n)** typical with sorting) and never looks back. DP considers every subproblem and is needed when a locally optimal choice can lead to a globally worse result.

cards.english: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's algorithm).
cards.grammarNote: **Kadane's**: extend the running sum, but restart at n whenever the previous sum is negative (it can only drag you down). Track the best seen. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

cards.english: Jump Game — can you reach the last index?
cards.grammarNote: Work backwards, tracking the leftmost index that can still reach the end. If a cell can jump to the current goal, it becomes the new goal. Reachable iff the goal shrinks to 0. **O(n)** time.

cards.english: What's the usual first step for interval problems?
cards.word: Sort by start time (sometimes end) — O(n log n)
cards.grammarNote: Almost every interval problem begins by **sorting** by start (or end) so overlaps become adjacent and you can sweep left to right in one pass. The sort dominates at **O(n log n)**.

cards.english: How do you test whether two intervals overlap?
cards.word: a.start <= b.end && b.start <= a.end
cards.grammarNote: Two intervals overlap iff each starts before the other ends. Equivalently, they **don't** overlap when one ends before the other begins. This check drives merging, insertion, and conflict counting.

cards.english: Insert Interval — insert and merge into a sorted, non-overlapping list.
cards.grammarNote: Three phases: copy intervals ending before the new one, **merge** all that overlap it, then copy the rest. Input is already sorted, so it's **O(n)**.

cards.english: Merge Intervals — merge all overlapping intervals.
cards.grammarNote: **Sort by start**, then sweep: if the next interval starts within the last merged one, extend its end; otherwise begin a new interval. **O(n log n)** time (the sort).

cards.english: Non-Overlapping Intervals — min removals to eliminate overlaps.
cards.grammarNote: Greedy: sort by start; on an overlap, drop the interval that **ends later** (keeping the earlier end leaves more room). Count the removals. **O(n log n)** time.

cards.english: Meeting Rooms — can one person attend all meetings?
cards.grammarNote: Sort by start; if any meeting starts before the previous one ends, they conflict. **O(n log n)** time.

cards.english: Meeting Rooms II — minimum number of rooms needed.
cards.grammarNote: Sweep-line: sort start and end times separately; step through them in order, +1 room on a start, −1 on an end. The peak concurrent count is the answer. **O(n log n)** time. (A min-heap of end times also works.)

cards.english: How do you rotate or transform a matrix in place?
cards.word: Compose simple ops: transpose + reverse rows = 90° rotation
cards.grammarNote: In-place matrix tricks avoid extra space by combining operations: **transpose then reverse each row** rotates 90° clockwise; using the first row/column as marker storage lets you flag zeros without an auxiliary matrix (**O(1)** extra space).

cards.english: What's the complexity of visiting every matrix cell?
cards.word: O(m·n) time; O(1) extra space if done in place
cards.grammarNote: Any full traversal (spiral, flood fill, marking) touches each of the m·n cells once → **O(m·n)** time. Many matrix problems can be solved with **O(1)** extra space by mutating the grid itself.

cards.english: Rotate Image — rotate an n×n matrix 90° clockwise in place.
cards.grammarNote: **Transpose** (swap across the diagonal) then **reverse each row** = 90° clockwise rotation, all in place. **O(n²)** time, **O(1)** extra space.

cards.english: Spiral Matrix — return elements in spiral order.
cards.grammarNote: Maintain four shrinking boundaries (top/bottom/left/right); traverse right→down→left→up, tightening each bound after its pass. The mid-loop break handles thin leftover strips. **O(m·n)** time.

cards.english: Set Matrix Zeroes — zero out each 0's row and column in place.
cards.grammarNote: Use the **first row and column as markers** to record which rows/cols must zero, with one extra flag for the first row itself. Gives **O(1)** extra space instead of O(m+n). **O(m·n)** time.

cards.english: What are the most useful bit tricks?
cards.word: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit; 1 << i, n & 1, n >> 1
cards.grammarNote: Key operations: **n & (n-1)** removes the lowest set bit (count bits, power-of-two check); **n & 1** tests the last bit; **1 << i** builds a mask; **>>** / **<<** shift. In JS, bitwise ops treat numbers as **32-bit signed** ints; use **>>> 0** for unsigned.

cards.english: What XOR properties show up in interviews?
cards.word: a^a = 0, a^0 = a, and XOR is commutative/associative
cards.grammarNote: Because a value XORed with itself cancels to 0, XOR-ing an array finds the **single** unpaired element or the **missing** number in O(n) time and O(1) space. XOR also swaps values and computes 'sum without carry'.

cards.english: Number of 1 Bits (Hamming weight).
cards.grammarNote: `n & (n-1)` removes the lowest set bit each iteration, so the loop runs once per 1-bit — **O(number of set bits)**, faster than checking all 32 bits.

cards.english: Counting Bits — set-bit count for every i in 0..n.
cards.grammarNote: DP on bits: i has the same upper bits as i>>1 plus its lowest bit (i&1). Builds all answers in **O(n)** time instead of O(n log n).

cards.english: Reverse Bits — reverse the 32 bits of an integer.
cards.grammarNote: Pull bits off the bottom of n and push them onto the bottom of res while shifting res left — res ends up mirrored. Use `>>>` and `>>> 0` for unsigned 32-bit behavior in JS. **O(32)** time.

cards.english: Missing Number — find the missing value in 0..n.
cards.grammarNote: XOR every index and every value together with n; each present number cancels with its index, leaving only the **missing** one. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space (no overflow, unlike the sum formula).

cards.english: Sum of Two Integers — add without + or -.
cards.grammarNote: XOR adds bits **without** carry; AND-then-shift finds the carry. Repeat until there's no carry left. **O(1)** (bounded by word size).
